On the word ἀστόξενος [townsman-stranger] see the passages of the grammarians in the Thesaurus vol. 1, 2, p. 2252, among whom is Pollux 3, 60: ἀστόξενος [townsman-stranger] according to some is the same as ἰδιοξένῳ [private guest-friend], according to others one who is a stranger by birth but a citizen by honor; to some it seems to be one who is a citizen by nature but a stranger in reputation, as Danaus to the Argives, having his descent from Io the Argive, who refers to Aeschylus Suppl. 356 εἴη δ᾽ ἄνατον πρᾶγμα τοῦτ᾽ ἀστοξένων [may this matter of the townsmen-strangers be without harm], which the scholiast explains as τῶν νῦν μὲν ξένων, πρώην δὲ συνημμένων τῷ ἄστει [of those now strangers, but formerly joined to the city].

ἀστόξενος [townsman-stranger]: one who does not have a private house among the citizens; rightly corrected to ἐν τῇ πόλει [in the city], comparing Hesychius' gloss ἀστόξενοι [townsmen-strangers]: those who do not have a private house in the city (τὴν [the] should be deleted).

The Ionic form ξεῖνος [stranger], which the tragedians do not seem to have used except when the meter required it, has one example in Aeschylus, Sept. 942, more in Sophocles and Euripides: on which I have spoken in the Lexicon Sophocleum p. 319. The meaning of the word is foreigner or guest, and it is used either adjectivally, as Ch. 730 ἁνὴρ ὁ ξένος [the stranger man], or, much more frequently, substantivally.
a foreigner, a guest
Frequent use of the vocative ξένε [stranger] or ξένοι [strangers] in address.
Feminine ξένη [stranger woman] a foreign woman.
